prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: EN · Issue tracker (language en).
Grid: 6 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "ID" · longest unbreakable word 39px · one-line width 75px
  col 2: header "Title" · longest unbreakable word 92px · one-line width 394px
  col 3: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 4: header "Assignee" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 66px
  col 5: header "Status" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 77px
  col 6: header "Updated" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 87px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"An issue tracker for quick triage: identify each issue, read its title, compare severity/status, and see who owns it and how recently it changed.","reading":"Readers scan left to right: ID anchors the row, Title carries the main meaning, Severity and Status support triage, Assignee and Updated form a right-side ownership/recency rail. Statuses and severities are compared vertically; titles are read as sentences.","groups":["ID + Title — row identity and description; Title should dominate the reading path","Severity + Status — triage state; short categorical values compared together","Assignee + Updated — ownership and recency; related right-hand metadata"],"keep_intact":["ID strings such as BUG-2041","Severity labels: Critical, High, Low","Assignee handles such as m.garcia and a.okafor","Updated dates","Status labels as semantic units where possible"],"may_wrap":["Title between words; row height can absorb two or three title lines","Status between words only in compressed metadata designs, never inside a word"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[96,250,80,87,98,108],"idea":"Protect every metadata value on one line and give all remaining width to Title, which wraps to two lines where needed."},{"name":"B","widths":[96,291,80,87,82,83],"idea":"Maximize Title width while compressing Status and Updated just enough to wrap at word boundaries, keeping all identifiers and single words unbroken."},{"name":"C","widths":[96,206,80,87,112,138],"idea":"Metadata-forward layout: give Status and Updated generous single-line space and let Title wrap more aggressively for readers who scan state and recency first."}]}
